planting.note: Direct sow in fall onto bare, exposed novaculite scree or lean rocky mineral soil in full sun; seed needs winter chilling, and seedlings overwinter as a flat rosette before flowering the second spring.

directions: This biennial mustard is known only from a handful of bare novaculite rock exposures and thin glade margins in the Ouachita Mountains of Arkansas, an even narrower habitat than the sandstone-novaculite mix used by its more widespread relative, clasping jewelflower. Tightly clasping, scale-shaped gray-green leaves wrap the erect second-year flowering stem, which is topped with the inflated, papery, maroon-tinted calyces typical of the genus in late spring. Because it is adapted to essentially bare rock with almost no soil buildup, give it extremely sharp drainage and skip soil amendment entirely, reproducing the thin mineral grit of its native outcrops in a dedicated rock garden tray or scree bed. Source seed only from regional conservation or native-plant programs, since wild colonies are small and scattered across just a few Ouachita peaks.

planting.note: Set out divisions or plugs in spring into humus-rich, well-drained soil in dappled shade beneath oak canopy, mirroring the forest openings and bottomland edges of its native Ouachita Mountains range.

directions: Ouachita bluet is a diminutive member of the coffee family restricted to oak forest openings and bottomland edges of the Ouachita Mountains of Arkansas and Oklahoma, where it forms loose, spreading tufts rather than the dense lawn-like mats of its common roadside cousin. From April into early June it bears small, four-lobed, pale blue-white flowers held just above narrow basal leaves, favoring the dappled light and leaf-litter soil of open woodland rather than full sun. Plant it in humus-rich, evenly moist but well-drained soil under high deciduous shade, and let it spread gently at the front of a native shade border or woodland path edge. Divide congested clumps in spring and source stock only from nursery or seed-grown regional material given its narrow native range.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring or fall into rich, humus-laden soil on a shaded, steep slope, reproducing the mesic hardwood ravine banks of the Ouachita Mountains where this sedge grows wild.

directions: This fine-leaved tufted sedge is endemic to steep, shaded slopes within rich mesic to dry-mesic hardwood ravines of the Ouachita Mountains of Arkansas and Oklahoma, a narrower habitat than the dry woodland edges favored by many of its more common Carex relatives. It forms a low, graceful clump of narrow, arching foliage on slender three-angled stems, staying under about 16 inches tall and spreading gradually by short rhizomes rather than aggressive runners. Because it comes from steep forested slopes with constant leaf-litter moisture, give it consistently humus-rich, well-drained soil in deep to partial shade rather than the drier conditions many woodland sedges tolerate. It makes a fitting small-scale native ground cover for a shaded ravine-style planting or woodland rock garden rather than a general-purpose lawn substitute.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring into humus-rich, moisture-retentive soil on a shaded north-facing slope beneath deciduous canopy, the specific mesic forest setting this goldenrod occupies in the wild.

directions: Unlike the sun-loving prairie goldenrods most gardeners know, this species is a true forest-interior goldenrod confined to mesic, north-facing wooded slopes scattered through the Ouachita Mountains of Arkansas and Oklahoma. Upright, leafy stems rise from a slowly spreading rhizome and carry narrow, pointed leaves topped by loose, arching plumes of small yellow flowers from September into October, later than most woodland wildflowers finish blooming. Because it comes from consistently shaded, humus-rich mesic sites rather than open ground, plant it under high deciduous canopy in evenly moist, well-drained soil and avoid the baking full-sun exposure that suits most other goldenrods. Its late fall bloom makes it a valuable extended nectar source for woodland-edge pollinators after most shade perennials have finished for the year.

planting.note: Plant dormant rhizome divisions in fall into deep, humus-rich ravine-floor soil in full shade, matching the undisturbed leaf-litter conditions of mesic Ouachita Mountain ravines where this toothwort grows wild.

directions: This regional variety of slender toothwort is restricted to rich, mesic ravines within the Ouachita Mountains, distinguished from the more widespread form of the species mainly by narrower, more finely cut leaflets. Like other toothworts it is a true spring ephemeral, pushing up deeply divided, ternate foliage and loose clusters of small white to pale pink four-petaled flowers in March and April before going fully dormant underground by early summer. Plant rhizome pieces in deep, consistently moist, humus-rich soil under full canopy shade and leave the planting undisturbed, since toothworts spread slowly and resent frequent digging. It pairs naturally with other Ouachita ravine ephemerals as an early-season ground layer that disappears gracefully once the forest canopy closes overhead.

planting.note: Sow seed in fall onto consistently moist, humus-rich ravine soil in deep shade, since seed needs a full winter of cold, moist stratification to germinate the following spring.

directions: One of the more recently recognized Ouachita Mountain endemics, this waterleaf occupies rich, consistently moist mesic ravine forests and is closely related to the more widespread eastern waterleaf species already familiar to shade gardeners. It produces mottled, lance-shaped foliage typical of the genus and coiled clusters of small, bell-shaped white to pale lavender flowers in April and May, then dies back to the roots by midsummer like many spring woodland perennials. Because its wild populations are confined to a small number of shaded ravine drainages, give it deep, humus-rich soil that stays reliably moist through spring, under full canopy shade rather than the drier woodland edges many native wildflowers tolerate. Grow it from nursery- or seed-propagated stock rather than wild-collected material given how geographically limited the species remains.
